scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

There’s no one-size-fits-all answer, but I’ll break this down with **honesty, empathy, and ethical considerations**—because your question isn’t just about "right" or "wrong" in a moral sense, but about **boundaries, self-preservation, and family dynamics**. --- ### **1. Is This "Right" or "Wrong"?** **Neither.** It’s a **moral gray area** that depends on: - **Your mental health and safety** (the *primary* consideration). - **The impact on others** (especially your parents, who are already hurting). - **The long-term health of your relationships** (with your dad, sister, and family). This isn’t a "punishment" for your sister—it’s **self-care in the face of chronic emotional harm**. But the *how* matters. --- ### **2. Why This Situation Feels So Guilty** You’re grappling with **three conflicting loyalties**: 1. **Your sister’s feelings** (even though she’s abusive, you may fear hurting her). 2. **Your parents’ expectations** (they want you to "try harder" with her). 3. **Your own needs** (you’ve worked hard to heal, and this is a small but meaningful step). This guilt is **valid**, but it’s also **misplaced** in a few ways: - **You’re not responsible for her emotions**—her fragility isn’t your burden to carry. - **Your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" is well-intentioned but flawed**—they’re asking you to sacrifice your healing for someone who can’t reciprocate. - **Your sister’s absence is an opportunity**, not a betrayal. You’re not "choosing" her; she’s choosing to be away. --- ### **3. Ethical Considerations** #### **A. Is It Fair to Your Dad?** - **No, if you’re lying or misleading him.** If you tell him you’re skipping because of a "scheduling conflict" (which is true) but *also* know your sister’s absence is the real reason, that’s a stretch. But if you’re **honest** (e.g., *"I’d love to see you, but my husband and I have a family thing that weekend"*), that’s fair. - **Yes, if you’re being transparent about your limits.** Your dad deserves to know you’re struggling with your sister’s presence. He might not like it, but he’ll respect your honesty. #### **B. Is It Fair to Your Sister?** - **No, if you’re using her absence as an excuse to avoid her entirely.** That would be manipulative. - **Yes, if you’re using it as a *temporary* boundary** while you figure out how to interact with her in the future. This isn’t about punishing her—it’s about protecting yourself. #### **C. Is It Fair to Your Parents?** - **No, if you’re keeping this a secret.** They’ve already been hurt by your sister’s behavior; hiding this would add another layer of pain. - **Yes, if you frame it as a *necessary* boundary for your healing.** Example: > *"Mom, Dad, I love you both, and I want to be there for you. But I’ve been doing a lot of work on my mental health, and spending time with [sister] is really hard for me right now. I’m not sure I can be fully present at the party this year, but I’d love to see you both separately."* --- ### **4. What Would Be the *Healthiest* Approach?** #### **Option 1: The "Honest Boundary" (Best for Long-Term Trust)** - **Attend the party, but set clear limits.** - Example: *"I’ll be there, but I might step out if things get overwhelming."* - Bring your husband for support (if he’s okay with it). - If your sister lashes out, **you’re allowed to leave**. No guilt. - **Have a separate conversation with your dad** (privately) about how her presence affects you. He might not like it, but he’ll understand you’re prioritizing your well-being. #### **Option 2: The "Strategic Absence" (If You Can’t Tolerate Her Presence)** - **Skip the party, but be transparent with your parents.** - Frame it as a **temporary step** while you work on your healing. - Example: *"I’m not feeling up to the party this year, but I’ll be there next time when things are calmer."* - Offer to **help plan a separate celebration for Dad** (e.g., a smaller gathering without your sister). - **This is riskier** because it might hurt your parents, but it’s **honest and necessary** if you can’t be around her. #### **Option 3: The "Compromise" (If You Want to Minimize Conflict)** - **Attend the party, but limit interaction with your sister.** - Sit far away, keep conversations brief, and have an "exit plan." - If she’s there, **you don’t owe her your full attention**. It’s okay to engage politely but not deeply. - **This is a middle ground**—not perfect, but better than forcing yourself to endure her abuse. --- ### **5. Why You Might Feel Like You’re "Choosing" Your Sister** This is a **common trap** when dealing with family dynamics: - **Abusers (even unintentionally) create a sense of obligation.** You might feel guilty for "abandoning" her, but that’s her manipulation, not your responsibility. - **Your parents’ love for her is misplaced.** They’re afraid of her, not of you. Their fear isn’t a reason to stay in harm’s way. - **Your healing is *not* selfish.** It’s **necessary**. You can’t pour from an empty cup. --- ### **6. What Your Parents Might Need to Hear** If you’re open to talking to them, try: > *"I love you both, and I want to be part of our family. But I’ve been doing a lot of work on my mental health, and being around [sister] is really hard for me. I’m not sure I can be fully present at the party this year, but I’d love to see you both separately. I’m not giving up on her—I’m just taking care of myself first."* This **shifts the focus to your needs** without blaming her or them. --- ### **7. Final Verdict: Is This AITA?** **No, if:** ✅ You’re being **honest** with yourself and your family. ✅ You’re **not using her absence as an excuse to avoid her entirely** (this would be unfair). ✅ You’re **prioritizing your mental health**, which is **not selfish**—it’s **survival**. **Yes, if:** ❌ You’re **lying to your dad** or **keeping this a secret** from your parents. ❌ You’re **using this as a permanent excuse** to avoid her (boundaries are temporary; cutting her out entirely is a different choice). ❌ You’re **feeling guilty for setting limits**, which suggests you haven’t fully accepted that her behavior is **not your fault**. --- ### **8. What’s the *Real* Question?** This isn’t just about **one birthday party**—it’s about **how much you’re willing to tolerate**. Ask yourself: - **Can I be around her without feeling drained or anxious?** - **Is there a way to interact with her that doesn’t trigger me?** - **Am I doing this for me, or because I feel guilty?** If the answer is **"No"** to the first two, then **your needs come first**. If you’re doing this out of guilt, then **you need to process that guilt**—it’s a sign you still need to set firmer boundaries. --- ### **9. A Final Thought: You’re Not a Bad Daughter** You’re **not obligated to endure abuse** just because it’s "family." Your parents’ love for your sister doesn’t erase the fact that **she’s harmed you**. Your healing is **not a betrayal**—it’s **survival**. If you decide to skip the party, **own it**. If you decide to attend but with limits, **own that too**. Either way, you’re making a **courageous choice**—one that prioritizes your well-being over others’ expectations. --- ### **TL;DR:** - **You’re not wrong for prioritizing your mental health**, but **how you communicate it matters**. - **If you skip the party, be honest with your parents**—don’t lie or hide it. - **If you attend, set clear boundaries** and don’t feel guilty for protecting yourself. - **This isn’t about "choosing" your sister—it’s about recognizing that her behavior is not your responsibility.** You’re doing the right thing by **listening to your needs**. The rest is about **how you navigate the fallout**—and that’s something only *you* can decide. 💛 *(And hey—first-time poster! Welcome to the community. This is a really brave question to ask.)*
